children: By Krishna Pokharel and Tripti Lahiri
The number of people missing in catastrophic floods in Nepal and China rose to 3,000, nearly a third of them workers stationed at power projects in Nepal.

More than 630 people have been declared dead after the flood hit Nepal's northern border regions and China's Tibetan areas, sparked by what scientists believe was the collapse of part of a glacier and the bedrock underneath. The rock-ice avalanche crashed thousands of feet into the valley below, where it was pulverized into a muddy debris-laden flood.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on Saturday that 626 bodies had been recovered. In China, authorities said that seven people have died.
More than 2,400 people are missing in Nepal, including 934 workers linked to power projects in operation or under construction, built as part of a hydroelectricity boom in the Himalayan country.

Construction across mountains in South Asia is placing more workers in risky terrain that is being destabilized by warming temperatures. When disaster hits, many of these workers are the first in harm's way.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a Facebook post that rescue efforts are focusing on these workers, some of whom are trapped in tunnels.
A team led by Nepal's army dug through thick mud earlier this week and were able to pull out some 350 workers and locals trapped in a tunnel of a project on the Trishuli River, video showed.
Army personnel lowered themselves from the helicopter and clambered up a muddy slope to pull out people covered in mud. Survivors were hauled back up in baskets into the helicopter.
On Saturday, 90 workers were rescued from another hydropower site, according to the chief executive of Nepal's power producers' association.
More than 500 foreign tourists, including 65 Americans, are also among the missing.
In China, more than 550 people are missing, about half of them foreign tourists, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Nepal has declined search-and-rescue help but said it needs technical assistance and machinery.

Nepal's Tourism Board on Saturday shared on its Facebook page a list of equipment requested by the local authorities in Rasuwa district, including body bags, pulleys and personal protective equipment.

Rescue operations continued on Saturday at Gyirong Port, a customs and immigration checkpoint on China's side of the land crossing with Nepal. Satellite imagery indicates the port buildings have been almost completely razed.

In a video shared on Xinhua's X account on Saturday, Chinese rescuers were seen searching in the morning for survivors through the mud and debris of rocks and vehicles in the checkpoint area with probing rods.
